newsitem.title: UK: IPE looks to expand further into non-oil energy.
newsitem.headline: IPE looks to expand further into non-oil energy.

text.p: London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) is examining the options for expanding natural gas trading into continental Europe and opening an electricity contract, a spokeswoman said on Tuesday.
A month and a half after launching Europe's first natural gas futures contract the IPE was looking at ways to move from oil into more new energy futures contracts.
Research into an electricity contract was sparked "by a lot of interest" but no timetable had yet been set for a possible launch, the spokeswoman said.
Other exchanges also were considering development of electricity futures, she said. "We would have to be the first. There's no point in being the second."
Various options were open for expanding the IPE's natural gas contract to cover continental Europe when the Interconnector pipeline from Britain to Belgium opens late next year, the spokeswoman said.

The natural gas contract so far operates only within the UK, and is based on physical delivery at the National Balancing Point, a notional point on the trunk pipeline system so that gas has already paid the entry costs for coming onshore and into the pipeline.

But the IPE was keen to expand this. "We've always seen it as a European contract. The UK is too small to support a contract," the spokeswoman said. "When the Interconnector comes in, we expect to see several price benchmarks appearing, one of which may take the lead."
Belgian Zeebrugge and Aachen were possibilities, she said.
A contract based at Bacton, less exclusive to the British market than the NBP and better suited to pan-European trade, was described as "ready to roll."

But there were still problems to be resolved over claims validation at Bacton, the procedure by which counterparties to a trade can determine that gas has been delivered at a particular location as specified in the contract.
Suggestions for a coal contract were "not a front runner," she said.
Speculative discussion also had raised the possibility of a high sulphur fuel oil contract.
